title: Making up a story in play
keyIdea: When you play with toys, you can make up your own story. Start with story words such as "Once upon a time". Let each toy talk and act like itself. Make something happen, an "oh no!", and let someone fix it. Then finish with an ending, "The end". Change the toys, the place or the problem, and you have a new story.
familyTip: Join the play as a character, not the director. Start with "Once upon a time…", give your toy a voice, then pause and ask "Oh no, what happens next?" Let your child choose. When the play drifts, offer an ending: "And then they all went home. The end!"

visual.caption: Does this start a story or end it? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: They all went home for tea. The end.
One day, a little red car…
And they all went to sleep.
Long ago, in a big dark wood…
Hooray! The hat was back. The end.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: start a toy story with story words, give each toy its voice, make an oh no and fix it, find an ending, then mix cards to make up new stories.

kid: You can make up a story when you play. Start with story words. Say: "Once upon a time…"
Your toys can talk! A big dragon says ROAR. A tiny mouse says squeak. Each toy talks like itself.
Then something happens. Oh no! The hat blows up a tree. Who can help? The dragon can fly up and get it.
A story stops at an end. Say: "They all went home. The end." Then make up a new one!
adult: Ages 3 to 4. Development Matters (2021) expects 3 and 4 year olds to begin to develop complex stories using small-world equipment such as animal sets, dolls and dolls houses, to use longer sentences and to tell a long story. By the end of Reception the Speaking goal asks children to invent, adapt and recount narratives and stories with peers and their teacher. Making up a story in play is where that inventing starts: the child puts known story language to work on toys, rather than only retelling a book.

At this age a story needs four simple parts. There is an opening, such as "Once upon a time" or "One day". There is a character who talks and acts in a way that fits it. Something happens, a problem or "oh no", and it gets fixed. Then there is an ending. Research on how young children tell stories (Applebee, 1978; Stein and Glenn's story grammar) shows the same step. Children move from a heap of events that do not link up to a simple chain with a problem and a way out.

Common mistakes: using an ending phrase at the start; play where toys move about but nothing happens; "and then… and then…" stories that never stop; walking away mid-story; a character doing something it could not do; and the belief that there is one right story, so the child only repeats a book. Be careful not to take over: join as a character, ask "what happens next?", and let the child decide.

In the lab your child drags "Once upon a time" into a talk bubble and puts Teddy on a play mat. Next they give Dragon, Mouse and Teddy their own lines. Then the wind blows Teddy's hat up a tree, and they drag the toy who can fly to get it. They pick an ending. Last, they mix who, where, oh no and end cards to make up two new stories.

practice.hint: Which words do you hear at the very start of a book?
practice.explain: "Once upon a time" tells everyone a story is starting. "The end" is for the finish.

practice.prompt: You have {n} toys in your story. 1 more toy comes to play. How many toys now?
practice.hint: Count the toys, then count one more.
practice.explain: {n} toys and 1 more make {=n+1} toys in the story.

practice.prompt: A big dragon is in your story. What does it say?
practice.hint: Is a dragon big or small? Loud or quiet?
practice.explain: A big dragon talks in a big, loud voice: ROAR! Each toy talks like itself.

practice.prompt: You made up {n} stories today. You make up 1 more. How many stories?
practice.hint: Count the stories you made, then add the new one.
practice.explain: {n} stories and 1 new one make {=n+1}. You can make up lots of stories!

practice.prompt: Teddy sits and sits. What can make it a story?
practice.hint: What makes you want to know what comes next?
practice.explain: A story needs something to happen. Oh no, the hat blows away! Now we want to know what comes next.

pool.prompt: How do we finish a story?
choices: And then… and then… for ever
pool.hint: Which one tells us the story has stopped?
pool.explain: An ending tells everyone the story is done: they go home, the end.

pool.prompt: A tiny mouse is in your story. How does it talk?
pool.hint: Is a mouse big or tiny? Loud or quiet?
pool.explain: A tiny mouse has a tiny voice: squeak! In play, toys can talk.

pool.prompt: The hat is up a tall tree. Who in the story can get it?
pool.hint: Who in the story has wings and can go up high?
pool.explain: The dragon can fly up the tall tree. The tiny mouse cannot reach.

pool.prompt: Your story has {n} toys. 1 toy goes home. How many toys are left?
pool.hint: Count the toys, then take one away.
pool.explain: {n} toys, take away 1, leaves {=n-1} toys still in the story.

pool.prompt: Your friend made a robot story. You made a cat story. Who is right?
pool.hint: Is there just one story in the whole world?
pool.explain: Both! We can make up lots of different stories. There is no one right story.

pool.prompt: Which words can start a story?
pool.hint: Which words come at the very start, before anything happens?
pool.explain: "One day…" starts a story, just like "Once upon a time".

pool.prompt: Teddy has {n} hats. The wind blows 1 hat away. How many hats does Teddy have now?
pool.hint: Count the hats, then take one away.
pool.explain: {n} hats, take away 1, leaves {=n-1}. Oh no! Who can get it back?

pool.prompt: You want a new story. What can you change?
choices: Who is in it, or where it is
Nothing, it must be the same
pool.hint: What happens if a robot is in space, not a cat in the woods?
pool.explain: Change who is in it, where it is, or the oh no, and you make up a brand new story.

pool.prompt: What comes in the middle of a story?
choices: Something happens, then it gets fixed
pool.hint: Start words come first, end words come last. What is in between?
pool.explain: In the middle, something happens (oh no!) and someone fixes it.
